extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and students of U.S. patent law (patent applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and procedural standards governing caveats and applications for U.S. letters-patent: who may apply, required contents and form of applications, the oath, evidentiary effect of caveats and oaths, confidentiality, renewals, and consequences of omissions or falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat term and renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: At the expiration of this term it may be renewed for another year by the payment of an additional fee; and so on from year to year during the pleasure of the caveator; if not renewed it still remains in the secret archives of the Office, although it ceases to secure any rights to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats are renewable annually upon fee payment; failure to renew ends the caveat's protective effect though the record remains in secret archives. Keep renewal payments current to preserve notice rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of subsequent interfering applications to caveator
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an application for a patent for the same invention is filed by a rival, either simultaneously with the caveat or during its life, and the invention described is found by the Office to be patentable and to correspond apparently with that specified in the caveat, proceedings on the application are suspended, the application (specification, drawings, model) is deposited in secret archives, and the caveator is notified to file his application so rival claims may be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notified, the caveator must present his application within three months from the expiration of the normal mail transmission time from Washington; if both applications claim the same invention an interference will be declared and heard. Maintain readiness to file promptly upon notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to give notice and effect of omission
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the Commissioner to give notice to the caveator; if through any fault or inadvertence in the Office the notice is omitted or the caveator fails to receive it, and a patent issues to the applicant, the latter can take no advantage from his patent in any subsequent interference proceeding between himself and the caveator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office must mail notice; accidental omission does not prejudice caveator's rights — in interference the patentee cannot benefit from a patent obtained where notice was not given due to Office fault. However, the Office is not strictly bound to insure receipt beyond ordinary mailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of caveat-notice protection (timing limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule requiring notice applies exclusively to applications filed pending the caveat; of those already in the Office when the caveat is filed, and those presented after the life of the caveat expires, the caveator has no right to be informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat protects only later-filed rival applications during the caveat's life; it does not require retroactive notice of prior-filed or post-expiration filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats kept secret; fraudulent disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat is filed in the confidential archives of the Office and preserved in secrecy; fraudulent disclosure of a caveat to a rival applicant does not bar the rival's right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality is the rule, but courts have held that fraudulent disclosure does not automatically prevent the rival from obtaining a patent; remedies or consequences depend on circumstances (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat cannot be withdrawn; copies and amendments procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat, having been once filed in the Office, cannot be withdrawn by the caveator, either for the purpose of amendment or for any other purpose. Copies may be obtained in the usual manner; any correction or addition must be separately prepared and filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to withdraw or amend the original caveat in place — file separate corrective/additional documents as needed and obtain copies through official channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat as evidence of date (but not of completion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat is evidence of the date of the invention described therein and may be used in certain cases to prove that the inventive act had been performed before the time when it was filed; but unless necessarily inferred it does not show the invention was then completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a caveat as proof of an earlier date of conception/disclosure, but not conclusive proof that the invention was reduced to finished, patentable form at that date. Additional proof may be required of reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat not assignable by statute (practical contracting workaround)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law makes no provision for the assignment of a caveat or of the right to notice it is intended to secure; the invention described may be transferred by contract obliging the inventor to proceed with application on behalf of the real owner; caveat may serve to identify the transferred invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect transfers via contract/assignment of the invention/patent rights rather than relying on statutory assignment of the caveat itself; record and contractual arrangements should protect the assignee's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveator not concluded by caveat description
rubrics_metrics.description: The description given in a caveat is not conclusive upon the inventor or his assignee; it does not purport to be an account of a result accomplished but of a result expected and desired; the inventor may complete and vary the invention and, with due diligence, secure a patent for the matured invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a caveat is precautionary and does not estop the inventor from later perfecting the invention beyond the caveat's description; priority disputes remain focused on priority of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application must be made by the inventor (or proper legal representative)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a patent must in all cases be made by the inventor, if living, whoever may by law be actually entitled to the ownership when granted; if deceased after completing the invention, application must be made by executor or administrator in interest of heirs or assignees; joint inventions must be applied for by all joint inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedural origin of measures to obtain a patent must be by the inventor unless impossible; ensure correct applicant identity (inventor, representative, or joint inventors) in application filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office recognizes record title only
rubrics_metrics.description: In receiving and examining applications the Patent Office deals only with those who appear by the records of the Office to be the proper applicants; it has no jurisdiction over questions of title between rival claimants and must be guided entirely by the record title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve private title disputes externally; ensure assignments and record changes are properly filed and recorded with the Office to be recognized in prosecution and at issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications must conform to statutory/legal requirements; presumption from grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Every application must conform in all respects to the requirements of the law; the Patent Office has no power to dispense with them. From the granting of the patent courts presume all formal requirements have been fulfilled, and this presumption is not lightly disturbed except in proceedings to repeal the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply strictly with statutory prerequisites; although the courts will presume compliance when patent is issued, formal defects can render a patent void and may be attacked in appropriate proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and completeness of application (writing, language, contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application and all communications with the Office must be in writing, correctly, legibly, and clearly written; the Commissioner may require them to be printed at party's cost. The application must be in English, addressed to the Commissioner, and include a petition, an oath, and a specification or Description and Claim; in certain cases it must be accompanied by drawings and a model or specimen. No application can be accepted for examination until complete in all its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare complete, legible, English-language filings with petition, oath, specification and claims, and any required drawings/models; unsigned, blank, altered, or partly filled applications may be stricken if irregularity discovered before grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must be a communication addressed to the Commissioner, duly signed by the applicant, requesting grant of letters-patent; it must state the name and residence of the petitioner and must contain words of reference to the specification for fuller disclosure of the invention. It should set forth the person on whose behalf the application is made and to whom the patent is desired to issue, declaring whether to the applicant himself or to an assignee or joint owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the petition identifies applicant/residence, references the specification, and declares the intended patentee(s) (applicant/assignee/joint holders) to avoid identification problems in prosecution and at issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application oath: who may take and where
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath must be made by the inventor if alive, or by his personal representative if he is dead; it can be taken before any person in the United States authorized to administer oaths, or when the applicant resides in a foreign country, before ministers, chargés d'affaires, consuls, commercial agents holding commission under the United States, or before a notary public, the oath being attested by the official seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the oath only before authorized officers and obtain required attestation/seal for foreign oaths; missing or improper attestation can invalidate the procedural requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application oath: required averments
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must swear that he verily believes himself to be the original and first inventor of the art or instrument; that he does not know or believe the same was ever before known or used; that the invention has not been in public use nor on sale in the United States for more than two years preceding the application. He must also aver citizenship and place of residence and disclose names, numbers, and dates of any foreign patents for the same invention. The oath relates to the entire specification, and a new oath is required when new matter is added by amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the oath contains the statutory averments (originality, prior use/sale within two years, citizenship/residence, foreign patents) and refile oath when introducing new material by amendment. Incomplete disclosures of foreign patents or omitted averments can cause procedural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of oath's truth and consequences of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath's averments concerning originality relate only to the applicant's belief and are not necessarily false if prior knowledge is later discovered; however, a willfully false oath concerning citizenship or any other matter made essential by statute is a fraud upon the government and renders the patent void. After a patent issues the Patent Office has no jurisdiction to inquire whether the oath was true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid willful false statements in the oath (especially citizenship); honest mistakes about prior knowledge may not void a patent, but fraudulent averments are fatal. Challenges to the oath's truth typically require appropriate post-issuance proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary effect of the application-oath
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath is prima facie evidence that the applicant is the first and true inventor and in uncontested Patent Office cases is conclusive on matters to which it relates. When rival applications containing contradictory oaths exist, they nullify each other and further proof is open to determine priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the oath as strong initial evidence of priority and originality; in contested situations anticipate that contradictory oaths shift dispute to evidentiary proof and potential interference proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model/drawings and physical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain cases the specification must be accompanied by drawings and a model or specimen of the invention; parts of the model may be necessary which the applicant is not the first and original inventor of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide required drawings/models where statute or Office practice requires; note that models may involve components not solely created by the applicant and that the oath does not necessarily extend to the model.
